item.title: Barriers to Reporting Domestic Violence in Rural Areas
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Barriers to Reporting Domestic Violence in Rural Areas

The psychology of suffering in silence instead of calling for help.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Lengthy service provider response times discourage reporting abuse in remote areas.
  • In small towns, people can have confidentiality concerns, which can dissuade reporting.
  • Rural community leaders are often role models, committed to helping victims of abuse.

Domestic violence is an insidious form of interpersonal abuse, often invisible to others as it occurs behind closed doors. There are both physical and psychological barriers to detecting domestic violence in rural areas, where lower reporting rates obscure often rampant abuse. Yet smaller jurisdictions may also create an environment where community members experience a greater willingness to help. Research explains.

Source: Image by Ruslan Sikunov from Pixabay

Violence Prevalence and Response in Rural and Remote Areas

Joakim Petersson et al. (2025) examined the experiences of police officers and social workers responding to cases of intimate partner violence (IPV) within remote and rural areas of Sweden.[i] Analyzing interview data from 38 social workers and 6 police officers from six rural and remote regions, examining inter and intra-agency collaboration and risk management response, they found an incongruence between urban-centric IPV prevention policies and the unique cultural and structural characteristics of sparsely populated regions.

Although research is mixed regarding IPV prevalence rates in urban, rural, and remote areas, Petersson et al. recognize that service providers in rural and remote areas operate with fewer resources and less staff who are adequately trained to respond to IPV.[ii] This requires existing staff to respond to a larger area and cover a wider range of social problems without being able to specialize in any specific area. This is unfortunate because Petersson et al. note that rural and remote victims may engage in less help-seeking when exposed to IPV, which means they may suffer abuse that is more severe, enduring, and frequent.

A Lack of Local Service Providers

Petersson et al. acknowledge there are several reasons that victims in sparsely populated areas are less inclined to report, including practical and socio-cultural barriers which are unique to rural and remote areas. One practical reason is limited access to available service providers in areas that are rural and remote, because in such areas, law enforcement, healthcare providers, and shelters are few and far apart, if they exist in the area at all.

They also note that services may be impracticable to access due to distance, because service providers in sparsely populated areas may be gathered in regional hubs that are difficult to access. Poor infrastructure such as limited bus schedules may further complicate victims seeking help, assuming they can even leave an abusive home where they may be raising children themselves without assistance. For police, geography can cause delayed response times in responding to the calls for help they receive.

article continues after advertisement

Cultural and Gender-Based Views of IPV

Regarding socio-cultural challenges, Petersson et al. explain that reporting may be discouraged due to perceived social isolation, cultural norms of considering IPV to be a private matter and having a higher distrust of social agencies than experienced by victims in more urban areas.

They note that isolated and close-knit communities may hold patriarchal views about traditional gender roles, promoting beliefs that women are expected to stay at home and be obedient to their husbands. They recognize that such “rural masculinity” or “rural patriarchy” can normalize IPV and create reluctance for victims to reach out or engage with service providers.

A City Where Everyone Knows Your Name: Victim Reluctance and Community Response

Another barrier to reporting IPV in remote jurisdictions stems from the reality that like in the television sitcom Cheers, in a small town, everyone knows your name. Consequently, many victims are reluctant to report abuse due to concerns with confidentiality. Petersson et al. recognize this challenge as well, noting the lack of confidentiality may cause shame and embarrassment for victims, particularly when local service providers are also community members, who are often acquainted with both the victim and perpetrator.

article continues after advertisement

There was, however, one positive aspect to their research that stood in contrast to previous studies. Petersson et al. found that informal social control in sparsely populated areas may result in a friendlier community compared to urban areas. Although informal social control in remote areas may serve as a barrier for reporting, it may also provide an incentive to protect victims of IPV. They cite the importance of community leaders serving as role models along with social marketing campaigns designed to increase bystander intervention in rural areas. Such efforts can improve detection of abuse, provide aid to victims, and ensure that justice is served.

item.title: The Intersection of Motherhood, Mental Health, and Addiction
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

The Intersection of Motherhood, Mental Health, and Addiction

For women, mental health problems and addiction pose greater risks.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Mental health issues for women are complicated.
  • Addiction and mental health go hand in hand for women.
  • Postpartum mood issues are underdiagnosed and undertreated.

Woke up this morning to tragic news that is becoming all too familiar. Actress Hayden Panettiere is dead at age 36.

Panettiere, by what anyone could see, had all the gifts. A beautiful and popular actress who was also known as a talented singer. She played the titular character in the early 2000s rom-com "I Love You Beth Cooper", along with a role in TV shows "Heroes" and "Nashville." She consistently won Teen Choice and People's Choice awards and dabbled in activism and politics. She dated many actors and superstars and eventually gave birth to a daughter shared with boxing star Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. This seemed to be a turning point for her, with her eventually sharing with the world her struggles with postpartum depression, commenting on "Kelly and Michael" that her experience was "scary" and that postpartum mood issues deserved more attention. Sadly, Hayden eventually gave up full custody of her daughter to Klitschko in 2018, secondary to depression and addiction.

Understanding Deaths of Despair Among Young Adults

Whenever I hear of the death of someone in their 20s, 30s, or 40s, I always consider this a possibility of a death of despair. Economists have described these deaths as spikes in mortality in the United States related to overdoses, suicides, and medical complications related to addiction. Addiction and depression often go hand in hand. For women, the connection is very strong. Research into addiction in women demonstrates that women are at higher risk of becoming sicker more quickly; the medical problems that come from addiction show up earlier in women—i.e., liver disease, heart disease, cancer, and memory problems. Women also become addicted faster, a concept known as "telescoping." Telescoping is defined as the accelerated physiologic and clinical progression women commonly experience from initial substance use to full-blown addiction.

Another important point, specifically for Panettiere, whom I did not know nor treat and can only glean from what she has shared publicly, is that her postpartum depression was a significant issue. Postpartum mental health problems remain a misunderstood and understudied area of psychiatry and medicine, even in the 21st century. I started my professional life in the field of OBGYN and can attest that peri- and postpartum problems remain underdiagnosed and undertreated. It is an ironic tragedy that Lindsay Clancy is undergoing her murder trial in the Boston suburbs the same month that Panettiere was found dead. Clancy is the young mother and labor and delivery nurse who admitted to murdering her three children in 2023, 2 weeks after being released from arguably the best psychiatric hospital in the country. A review of court documents shows she struggled with severe postpartum mood swings and anxiety but was never formally diagnosed with it. Unfortunately, without a clear diagnosis, effective treatment is much harder to come by.

Challenges in Accessing Mental Health and Addiction Treatment for Women

Both of these women have heartbreaking stories. There are many other women who live quiet heartbreaks as well. For those women, who are not celebrities, treatment can be even more difficult to find. Adding to the complication, mental health disorders in women, whether they emerge in periods of hormonal fluctuations or are associated with psychosocial stressors or trauma, can become focal points for addiction to develop. Where I work, at a program that treats women specifically for both mental health and addictive disorders, 75-80 percent of women with addiction have experienced a trauma, with the trauma frequently precipitating the addiction.

article continues after advertisement

Access to care for women is a challenge, as women face a great risk of stigma when they admit to having struggles with mental health and addiction. Honestly reflect on your reaction to reading that Panettiere gave full custody of her daughter to her ex-partner. A bit shocking, right? Women are held to a higher standard as they are often seen as primary caregivers for children and elderly parents. Submitting their needs to care for others is a frequent barrier to care. Women also face demands and risks from social services; they face the real possibility that their children will be removed from their care if they need to seek treatment. Criminalization of drug use can direct women into the criminal justice system and possibly away from care as well.

What is the best answer to these issues? Research suggests that women benefit from gender-responsive care for addiction and mental health. Care that focuses on their unique psychological needs. Care in a protective environment that allows them to be vulnerable. Care that can address social needs, whether they be legal assistance, childcare, or social service help. Care that integrates a focus on the biological complications that women face in addiction, such as chronic pain and hormonal changes. All of these aspects of care can be integrated in a meaningful way to improve women's health. Improving women's health improves families and society as a whole. It is worth the effort.

item.title: Guess Where You Got Your Microbes
item.description:
Microbiome

Guess Where You Got Your Microbes

Nature goes to extremes to ensure you get some heirloom microbes.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Your microbiome is passed down from your mother at birth.
  • A healthy microbiome is important to support a healthy mental state.
  • There are three redundant mechanisms to ensure proper transmission of microbes.

“Only mothers can think of the future — because they give birth to it in their children.” —Maxim Gorky

The gut-brain axis depends on a healthy set of microbes — the microbiome — to generate a positive mood, clarity of thought, and a strong memory. That’s a major reason why nature goes to shocking lengths to pass on a microbiome.

Some insects, for instance, have special cells called bacteriocytes: fat cells that contain an entire microbiome in miniature, preserving the microbial heritage of the host insect. These bacteriocytes position themselves near the eggs, and during birth, the bacteriocytes burst and spill their precious cargo. Thus anointed, the eggs absorb the bacteria and begin the cycle anew.

These bacteria go to work immediately to scrounge nitrogen from the environment, providing vitamins and nutrients to the newborn larva. That ability to thrive on detritus has made insects — and their attendant microbes — some of nature’s most successful collaborations.

In the beginning

Some 1.5 billion years ago, animals formed and immediately recruited microbes to fight off pathogens and digest fiber. Animals and bacteria have some genes in common, and over time both the host and the bacteria dropped the redundant genes to become more efficient.

That had two important consequences:

  • The host became dependent on the microbes. For instance, humans no longer have the genetic machinery to create most vitamins — those jobs have been outsourced to microbes.
  • The microbes became dependent on the host. Because they lack essential genes, these bacteria could no longer live outside of the host and are no longer found in the environment.

That’s why passing down a microbiome is a biological imperative. There must be a mechanism to pass on this essential but vulnerable heritage, and — across the entire animal kingdom — that job typically falls to the mother.

Source: AI Generated

Humans are no exception. During pregnancy, the mother develops a distinctive vaginal microbiome, custom-built to anoint her baby. Certain lactobacillus species become dominant and the population becomes less diverse, amplifying microbes that are gut related. As you’re born, you get a healthy dose of these bacteria while squeezing down the birth canal.

Once born, you’re exposed to the outside world, which is cold, dry and highly infectious. You, of course, are naked. You have no real consciousness, and you won’t remember this day, but you know enough to cry.

Try not to think about it

Birthing can be an untidy business, and you are almost certain to pick up your mother’s fecal bacteria as well. Many animals pass on their microbes through mother’s poop, which is gross, but superbly efficient.

article continues after advertisement

This bacterial appetizer is there to kickstart your own microbiome and to teach your immune system what to tolerate. If your mother is in good health, you’ll get a lucky head start on life.

If you were born by caesarean, you missed a lot of that messy stuff. Instead, you were whisked away to a nursery where you picked up a bacterial population unique to your nurse’s gloves and your hospital room.

Some studies have shown that children delivered by C-section may lack important bacteroides species for up to the first 18 months of life, making them more likely to suffer from asthma and allergies. C-section babies seem to react differently to stress and are more susceptible to depression and anxiety, thanks to the gut-brain axis.

Not all outcomes are so bleak: new research has shown that at around six weeks, the microbiome of most of these children normalizes, with some of that due to breastfeeding. That’s because breast milk also contains microbes, carefully curated from the gut, that get passed down to the baby along with prebiotics to feed them.

The microbial triumvirate

These three inoculations, from the vagina, fecal matter, and breast milk, constitute your microbial starter kit, preowned and passed down from your mother, her mother, and her mother before her. Unless you become violently ill or take antibiotics in the first days of your existence, these bacteria will stick with you for life.

Which of these microbial samplers is most important? A recent Dutch study looked at 714 mother-baby pairs, from month 6 of pregnancy to 1 year old. They found that the major impact was the fecal route.

Such is life. It may start crappy but hopefully improves from there. Now that you know how you got one and why you need one, you might want to take better care of your microbial life partner. Feed it well. Your mind, mood, and memory depend on it.

item.title: Will AI Kill Creativity—or Set It Free?
item.description:
Creativity

Will AI Kill Creativity—or Set It Free?

AI has both positive and negative implications for our creative endeavors.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Artificial Intelligence can increase the creativity of select individuals.
  • However, AI often lowers collective creative diversity.
  • AI can become either a substitute, or a catalyst, for human creativity.

Suffice it to say, artificial intelligence (AI) has altered the creative landscape in several dramatic ways. Current figures indicate that about 24 percent of adults in the United States use AI chatbots daily. Beyond chatbots, 36 percent of Americans indicate that they interact with AI at least several times a day. This figure includes AI embedded in search engines, smartphones, social media, and smart devices. It would be safe to conclude that for a substantial portion of the American population, AI is a regular “cognitive partner” for brainstorming, problem-solving, crafting, and creating. And the numbers are rising.

This widespread usage raises the question embedded in this article’s title. That is, is AI an aid for our creative endeavors, or is it supplanting our natural creativity—the nonstop creative powers we had as youngsters? In response, let’s take a brief look at some compelling research.

What the Research Says

A 2024 creative writing experiment involved a group of 293 participants, each of whom was asked to write a short, eight-sentence story. The researchers noted that individuals who had access to AI-generated story ideas created narratives that were judged to be “more creative, better written, and more enjoyable.” This was particularly true for those subjects who were deemed to be less-creative writers. That said, there was also a notable trade-off—that is, AI-assisted stories were more similar to one another than those produced without the intervention of AI. The researchers’ conclusion was that AI can raise individual creativity while, at the same time, lowering the creative diversity of a group.

A prepublication research paper (2024/2025) described an experiment in which 800 individuals were introduced to either human-generated or ChatGPT-generated ideas and then asked to generate ideas of their own. The results were nothing short of amazing. That is, the researchers found that exposure to a high volume of AI-generated ideas did not necessarily improve the creativity of individual ideas, but it did affect the collective evolution of ideas. Their conclusion was that AI made ideas different, but not necessarily better.

A preprint/meta-analysis (2025) of 28 empirical studies involving 8,214 subjects found some evidence that AI can improve human creative performance. The effect was modest, but statistically meaningful. The researchers also discovered a compelling counter-effect; that is, there was a substantial decline in idea diversity when AI was used to generate new concepts. The final conclusion was that AI is a tool that can help create more innovative ideas while, at the same time, ideas that are more alike than different.

These studies, along with several others, underscore an intriguing question: When everyone has access to the same creative partner (such as ChatGPT), are we all now more creative, or are we all thinking the same?

Implications

Source: AiCanvas / Pixabay

It seems reasonable to assume that there are both positives and negatives regarding the AI/creativity connection. The prevailing research suggests that AI, in and of itself, doesn’t necessarily make everyone more creative. Rather, AI seems to alter how creativity happens. In short, we can decide to use AI as a substitute for our own imaginative shortcomings, or we can use it as a catalyst for expanding our creative endeavors. But there are also downsides. Let’s take a look.

article continues after advertisement

How AI enhances creativity:

  • AI can become a creative partner—one able to generate multiple ideas or possibilities beyond the range or experience of a specific individual.
  • Steve Jobs once said, “Creativity is just connecting things”—specifically linking seemingly unrelated ideas. AI has the ability to collect information from diverse fields, allowing humans to envision a range of (normally) improbable possibilities.
  • When generating ideas, we often get stuck on the first thing that comes into our mind. AI, on the other hand, can assist humans in moving beyond those initial concepts by generating a plethora of previously unconsidered or unknown ideas.
  • Writers are quite familiar with the “blank page/blank screen syndrome”—that is, overcoming “mental inertia” at the beginning of a new project or fresh challenge. AI can give writers (and other creatives) a starting point that allows them to expand, modify, alter, or revise.
  • AI can be a rapid idea accelerator—that is, it can generate a wealth of creative possibilities in minutes rather than hours. Thus, we have access to many possibilities without a large investment of time.

How AI diminishes creativity:

  • With AI, the “ownership” of original and innovative ideas diminishes. The ideas generated are machine-based rather than human-conceived. The line between those two concepts diminishes, and we often wind up with ideas more artificial than personal.
  • For many creatives, part of the experience is in the struggle to discover, select, and modify ideas appropriate for a new challenge. AI removes that option—it “pre-selects” the “correct answer(s)” without human intervention or consideration.
  • Our “intellectual investment” is limited when using AI. That is to say, if we are comfortable with whatever AI offers in response to a question, then we give up the necessary cognitive “homework” that underpins creative thinking. In short, we may become intellectually lazy rather than creatively active.
  • AI, quite often, produces a creative “regression to the mean.” In other words, if everyone is using the same AI platform (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Grammarly, Gemini) for their writing, artistic work, advertising, or other creative endeavors, the resulting products all begin to look and sound the same. On the surface, it may look creative but actually reflect homogenized information.
  • AI “averages” creativity. AI relies on the input of large amounts of human-created material. As a result, the information it shares is often predictable assumptions, familiar patterns, popular conventions, rational solutions, or everyday logic. Those first few ideas may be more common than novel, and more familiar than distinct.

According to the American Psychological Association, creativity is “the ability to produce or develop original work, theories, techniques, or thoughts. A creative individual typically displays originality, imagination, and expressiveness.” Noteworthy in that definition is the term “creative individual”—an indication that creative expression is fundamentally a human trait, rather than one generated by machines. It also raises a commanding query: “What happens to our personal creativity when we regularly collaborate with artificial creativity?” Stay tuned.

item.title: The Alpha Fail: Debunking the Myth That Has Misled Men
item.description:
Leadership

The Alpha Fail: Debunking the Myth That Has Misled Men

Why leadership is less about dominance and more about earning trust.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • The alpha male ideal offers a narrow and misleading model of what it means to be a man and a leader.
  • Healthy masculinities are built on strength, empathy, cooperation and social connection.
  • Manhood need not be proved through dominance; it can be expressed through trust, courage and care.
  • Men can use their strength to protect and empower others without needing to dominate them.

Some ideas cement themselves into popular culture—the American dream, the tortured genius, the midlife crisis... And then there's the concept of the “alpha male”. Picture a wolf pack: one big, aggressive male at the top fighting off challengers and keeping everyone else in line. It makes for a neat story about power, hierarchy, and masculinity. There’s just one problem. It’s a poor description of how a wolf pack functions.

The term "alpha male" was popularised by the biologist David Mech's (1970) book The Wolf: The Ecology and Behaviour of an Endangered Species. The idea that a dominant and aggressive male leads the wolf pack is compelling. It’s also based on a misunderstanding.

The research underpinning the alpha male theory was based largely on wolves held in captivity. In the wild, wolf packs are typically organised into family units led by the parents of pups. As the biologist Marc Bekoff (2024) stresses, leading wolf packs and other groups of canine species isn’t about being highly domineering, aggressive, or violent. To his credit, Mech (1999) acknowledged the limitations of the original model and warned others not to propagate the mistake.

But the genie was out of the bottle.

Between the start of the 1970s and the 2020s, the use of the term "alpha male" in written publications increased by more than 1,000 percent. In the 1980s, primatologist Frans de Waal used the term liberally in his book Chimpanzee Politics (de Waal, 1982). De Waal would later recall with regret that the success of his book catapulted the "alpha male" idea far beyond the field of biology.

It was co-opted initially by Reagan-era Republican politicians in the US before catching the attention of thought leaders in the world of business. The intervening decades have seen a veritable library of books published offering to help the reader alpha-up. Take, for example, the Alpha Male Bible (Wayne, 2021) and its revised version, the Supreme Alpha Male Bible (Wayne, 2022). Yes, without a hint of irony, there’s a hierarchy when it comes to versions of books that promise to make you an alpha male. But the tools that men are being sold to resolve their problems are a destructive misdirection. It’s like offering a baseball bat to peel an orange: it feels powerful, but it creates a mess.

The problem with the "alpha male"

In a 2023 interview, de Waal debunked the idea that leaders of groups of primates are necessarily the strongest, meanest, and most intimidating. Instead, he noted that effective leaders protect the underdog, break up fights, and have a high level of empathy. He also stressed the importance of supporters and alliances: you can’t do it on your own. De Waal saw important parallels with human societies. Rather than relying on dominance, our leaders succeed through empathy, helping others, and forging alliances. This is a version of manhood that I describe as homo cooperans—being a co-creator, a contributor, and a champion of others.

article continues after advertisement

True leadership, whether in the boardroom, locker room, or living room, isn’t about forcing compliance; it’s about fostering cooperation. It’s about running through walls with people rather than pressing their backs against them. And yet the alpha myth continues to exert a strong influence on our understanding of manhood.

In a 2024 survey, 45% of men and 31% of women agreed: "You must be an 'alpha male' these days to get a partner" (Britto et al., 2024). The New Yorker recently described “alpha-ness” as the “official demeanour of American power” (Bethea, 2026). The article details the emergence of an industry promising to amplify men’s alpha credentials through demanding—and potentially degrading—retreats and residential courses. It’s emblematic of the confused messaging modern men face. Which brings us to an important question: what kind of man are we actually encouraging men to become?

The alpha myth tells men to dominate. The pack tells a different story.
Source: Patrice Schoefolt / Pexels

Wolves or sheepdogs?

The 2025 post-apocalyptic horror movie 28 Years Later, directed by Danny Boyle, picked up where its predecessors 28 Days Later and 28 Weeks Later left off. Large swathes of the population of the UK continue to be infected with the Rage Virus. As its name suggests, the virus leads to the infected engaging in instant, extreme and uncontrollable violence against anyone who hasn’t yet been infected. But the new movie introduced a novel twist: enter the "alpha."

article continues after advertisement

It transpires that the seemingly frenzied activity of the infected can be coordinated by hulkingly big males. The "alphas," as they are dubbed, represent the most dangerous and uncontrollable versions of the infected. One of them, Samson, is played by Chi Lewis-Parry, a 6'9" mixed martial arts fighter. Whereas a well-placed arrow (more sophisticated weapons are in short supply!) can stop a standard infected, one of the movie’s leading characters notes that it would take half a dozen to stop an alpha. On learning that these leaders of the infected are called "alphas," another character remarks: “You make them sound like stockbrokers… like Wall Street guys.” It’s clear that the alpha myth continues to exert a considerable influence on popular culture, including our imagining of a dystopian future. But there is another metaphor that offers men a very different choice.

Some ten years before the release of 28 Years Later, another movie entitled American Sniper was released. Directed by Clint Eastwood, it tells the story of Navy SEAL Chris Kyle, a decorated soldier who served several tours of duty during the Iraq War. In the movie, there is a scene that flashes back to Kyle’s upbringing and his father delivering what has become known as the "sheepdog speech" to him and his younger brother. The dialogue is intercut with images of Chris protecting his brother during a playground fight. Kyle’s father explains that there are three kinds of people: sheep, wolves, and sheepdogs. The sheep represent those who are more passive and unprepared for danger. Wolves exploit and harm others. Sheepdogs, however, are willing to use their strength and presence to protect the vulnerable.

The metaphor is imperfect, but it highlights an important point for boys and men: in everyday life, we face choices about how we act. We can choose to dominate others or to protect ourselves at the expense of others. We can also choose to use our strengths to support other people and contribute to something bigger than ourselves. The sheepdog doesn’t need to become a wolf to confront one.

Strength without dominance

Rejecting the alpha myth does not mean rejecting strength, ambition, courage, or competitiveness. Men don't need to become passive, agreeable, or endlessly accommodating. Strength can be a virtue. The question is what we do with it. A man can use physical strength to protect someone being bullied. He can use social influence to challenge harassment. He can use professional authority to create opportunities for others. He can use emotional strength to remain calm when everyone else is losing their heads. None of these require him to dominate the people around him. In fact, they require something considerably harder: self-control.

The alpha male promises men status through dominance. The sheepdog offers something more demanding: strength through responsibility. Perhaps this is the model of manhood we should be encouraging. Not men who need to be the biggest, loudest, or most intimidating person in the room. But men who are strong enough to protect without dominating, confident enough to collaborate, and secure enough to help others succeed. True leadership isn't about standing above people. It is about standing with them. The goal isn't to become the biggest wolf in the pack. It is to become the kind of man who can help others around them to feel seen, safe, and supported.

item.title: Have We Gone Too Far With Boundaries?
item.description:
Boundaries

Have We Gone Too Far With Boundaries?

The difference between protecting yourself and protecting yourself from connection.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Boundaries protect our well-being, but not every disappointment is a boundary violation.
  • Healthy relationships require boundaries, communication, accountability, and a willingness to repair.
  • The goal is wiser boundaries that are firm enough to protect and flexible enough to connect.

If I had to choose the defining psychological buzzword of this decade, it would be boundaries. It's a word I hear almost daily in my therapy room and increasingly in everyday conversations. But as its popularity has grown, I find myself asking: Do we all mean the same thing when we use it?

Why We’re Talking About Boundaries More Than Ever

Boundaries are the thresholds that define us. They are the limits we set around what we will accept and how we will respond when those limits are crossed. They are different from expectations, preferences, or attempts to control other people's behavior. Boundaries communicate: This is where I begin and where I end. They protect our values, our time, our bodies, our energy, and our emotional well-being.

Their rise in popularity is understandable, as we are coming from generations where healthy relational dynamics often didn't exist. Certain races and genders were expected to tolerate belittlement or abuse, and countless people were denied a voice in decisions about their own lives. Families and cultures often justified harmful behavior in the name of tradition, loyalty, or preserving social norms. A significant shift was needed.

When society begins correcting an imbalance, however, the pendulum often swings to the opposite extreme before settling somewhere healthier. In many ways, that's where we are now. Boundaries have become the language of self-respect and protection, and rightly so. We now have words for experiences that previous generations simply endured in silence.

Sometimes boundaries need to be firm and even rigid. In situations involving abuse, manipulation, or repeated disrespect, they can be life-saving. But there is a nuance I don't hear discussed often enough. Have we become so focused on protecting ourselves that we're beginning to lose some of our capacity for humanity, repair, and connection?

When Protection Becomes Avoidance

Increasingly, I notice that people aren't talking to each other when conflict arises. Instead of difficult conversations, there are blocked numbers, ghosting, cutting people off, or declaring that someone has "crossed a boundary." While there are certainly situations where ending contact is the healthiest choice, I also wonder whether the language of boundaries is sometimes being used to justify avoidance.

Not every hurt or uncomfortable interaction is a boundary violation. Sometimes it's simply the discomfort of being in relationship with another imperfect human being. Healthy relationships require more than boundaries. They require communication, curiosity, accountability, and a willingness to repair when things go wrong. If boundaries become steel walls rather than doors with locks, they may protect us from harm, but they can also keep intimacy out.

article continues after advertisement

During a session, a client shared that she was upset because a friend had cancelled dinner twice in the same month due to family emergencies. She described the cancellations as a "boundary violation" and explained that she had responded by blocking her friend, saying, "My boundaries mean I don't tolerate people who disappoint me."

This example illustrates how the language of boundaries can sometimes be misunderstood. The issue appeared to center on unmet expectations and emotional hurt rather than a genuine boundary violation. Although repeated cancellations can understandably be disappointing, cancelling plans due to emergencies is not a boundary violation.

Rather than viewing the situation solely through the lens of boundary setting, I supported the client in exploring her emotional response and identifying the needs and expectations underlying her disappointment.

The Goal Isn't Stronger Boundaries; It's Wiser Boundaries

Healthy boundaries require discernment. They help us distinguish between abuse and disappointment, disrespect and misunderstanding, and situations that require distance versus those that call for honest conversation. Boundaries are not intended to shield us from every uncomfortable emotion or justify ending relationships whenever others fall short of our expectations. The goal is not simply to have stronger boundaries, but wiser ones—boundaries that are both firm and flexible, protecting us without isolating us and allowing connection without self-abandonment. The challenge lies in knowing the difference.

article continues after advertisement

3 Considerations to Help You Tell the Difference

  1. Ask whether a core value or limit has been crossed. A boundary violation occurs when someone disregards a clearly established limit related to your safety, dignity, autonomy, or well-being. If the issue is primarily disappointment, unmet expectations, or a mistake, it may call for a conversation rather than a boundary.
  2. Consider the pattern, not just the incident. Healthy relationships include misunderstandings, mistakes, and competing priorities. A single lapse, especially when accompanied by accountability or a reasonable explanation, is very different from a repeated pattern of disrespect or disregard for your expressed limits.
  3. Notice what response the situation requires. Ask yourself: Do I need protection, or do I need communication? If your safety, values, or well-being are at risk, firmer boundaries or distance may be appropriate. If the issue stems from hurt feelings or differing expectations, an honest conversation is often the healthier first step.

item.title: How to Quiet Your Ego and Reconnect With the World
item.description:
Self-Help

How to Quiet Your Ego and Reconnect With the World

Notice ego-driven striving and reconnect with what matters.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Ego-driven striving can leave us feeling isolated, inadequate, and never satisfied.
  • Noticing the ego as one part of you can create space for greater perspective.
  • Asking why you are striving can reveal whether ego or something deeper is driving you.
  • Turning your attention outward can reduce self-focus and deepen your sense of connection.

I opened up my Instagram this morning and saw a reel suggesting that the best way to get followers is to stop telling stories and start "yapping." The instructions were to hold a camera to your face and "yap" about yourself and your life as if the person watching was in the room with you, just observing what's happening in your head. The instructions were clear: Don't just yap; make sure your yapping is curated. Pretend like you're yapping, but make sure there's a point that drives people to your page.

To be honest, my first response was: Oh, I better start yapping more. I'm not doing enough. What will I yap about? A yap a day will clearly get me where I need to go.

We live in a world that is an evolutionary mismatch for our "selfing." Humans evolved egos as protectors — probably around the time of the agricultural revolution, when we moved from hunting and gathering to farming and needed to start planning ahead, thinking about ourselves, worrying, and ruminating.

In his book The Curse of the Self, Mark Leary describes the ego as a mental apparatus for thinking consciously about ourselves — and argues that it evolved the way other adaptations like opposable thumbs evolved, to help us survive. Some evolutionary psychologists argue that this voice in our head — the one that comments, advises, and thinks about us — evolved to help us imagine consequences, compete for resources, mentally time travel, plan ahead, make deliberate decisions, compare alternatives, understand others' minds, and create cultures.

But there's an evolutionary mismatch — not unlike our fondness for sugar and fat making so many of us sick in environments now saturated with fat and salt. All of this internal and external yapping is making us unwell — well, at least it's making me unwell, to be egotistical about it.

We think about ourselves and the outcomes we strive for way too much. As a result, we feel alone in our heads, not good enough, like we'll "never get there." As a high-performing client — a person who is at the very top of her game — told me yesterday, "I keep thinking I should be doing more."

The key words there are I and doing. Those are clues that your ego is at work.

These days, when I think about ego, I think of the part of us that chases after being right, being seen, being blown up like a helium balloon so that we can rise higher than others — only to deflate and fall pathetically to the living room floor. Your ego is the part of you that comments all day long about yourself. It's self-referential, self-focused, and loves a good selfie.

Stop, just a moment. Is it commenting now? I bet it is. Mine is too.

The Ego Distorts Our Perception of Reality

When college students were asked to rate themselves against their peers on a long list of qualities, the overwhelming pattern was the same: People rate themselves better than average on almost everything. One of the classic versions of this research, Alicke's 1985 study using 40 trait adjectives, found that people consistently see themselves as more honest, more capable, more everything-good than the average person — a bias so reliable psychologists just call it the "better-than-average effect."

article continues after advertisement

The Ego Rises and Falls Like a Roller Coaster

When I interviewed Ron Siegel about his book The Extraordinary Act of Being Ordinary, he talked about how what goes up must come down. One minute we feel great about ourselves, like we're better than others; the next, we feel like losers, walking embarrassments. This is what drives our striving — in hopes that one day, our ego will make it, and stay there.

The Ego Keeps You Separate

The concept of emptiness in Buddhism is similar to the concept of self-as-process in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy — the ego believes that little voice in your head is you, negating the you that is in relationship, the you that is in nature, the you that is connected to your ancestors. And when you're stuck in your head, you miss out on this feeling of bigger interconnection — what Dan Siegel calls the "MWe," the me that is also we. As a result we feel lonely, even in a crowd, and feel like it is all up to us to figure things out.

So what can we do about this little ego that follows us around everywhere? Here are a few tips from psychology and contemplative practice.

Call It by Its True Name

In my favorite poem by Thich Nhat Hanh, "Please Call Me by My True Names," he asks us to recognize ourselves in all of it — both the pirate and the 12-year-old refugee girl he assaulted, both the frog and the grass-snake that silently approaches and devours it. You can call your ego by its true name by noticing it as only one part of you — a frog today, maybe a pirate tomorrow — but the true you is much bigger, more interconnected. Get out of your head for a minute and into this moment. Who are you, really? The voice that is telling you scary stories? The voice that tells you, you are better than them? Or something else?

Ask Yourself, Why Are You Running?

When I interviewed Jo Confino the co-author of Being with Business and co-host of the podcast The Way Out Is In, he offered this simple tip: Notice when you're striving, and ask yourself why. Why are you running? What is driving your drive for more, for different? Is it your ego? Or is it something deeper?

article continues after advertisement

Stop Yapping and Start Listening

The ego dissolves when we meld with others, so yap about yourself — in your head and out loud — a little less. Put down the selfie camera and the self-help book. Stop referencing everything back to you, and start putting your two eyes out into the world instead. What else do you see? What are you curious about? What's happening around you?

You Have More Than Enough Conditions to Be Happy

When the ego future-trips on you, remember this simple gatha from Thich Nhat Hanh: Right now — what are those conditions? That could snap you out of it.

item.title: Are You Living Under Your Adult Child’s Weather?
item.description:
Parenting

Are You Living Under Your Adult Child’s Weather?

When your adult child’s emotional storms control the climate of your own life.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Parents get so skilled at reading an adult child’s emotional weather that they lose touch with their own.
  • Constantly anticipating the next crisis or blowup may feel protective, but the focus is one person’s moods.
  • You can care deeply about your adult child’s storm without having to stand outside in it.

This post, in a manner of speaking, is about the weather. A father, we can call him Mike, told me something that sounded almost like a superpower. He said, “I can tell from the first three words of her text what kind of night we’re going to have.” To clarify, his 29-year-old daughter, Sophia, didn’t live with him, which was the striking part. Remarkably, she actually lived 40 miles away, yet Mike could detect an approaching storm before it arrived.

I asked Mike to explain this further, and he shared what happens when Sophia says, “Can I ask you something?” That often translates to a possible financial storm. Or when Sophia leads with “You’re probably going to say no, but…,” that forecasts a high probability of conflict. Now let's get to the doozy. Mike elaborated: "When Sophia says, 'Never mind,' I have come to see that as a severe emotional storm approaching."

The Most Ominous Forecast of All

Mike continued with his weather metaphor and said, "Dr. Jeff, I haven't even told you the most ominous forecast of all: That's when there are actually no texts from Sophia." Mike told me that Sophia's silence could send him into checking his phone every 15 minutes. Like many of my parent coaching clients, Mike had become extraordinarily good at predicting his adult child's "emotional weather." The problem was that he was no longer living in his own climate. When parents live in a hypervigilant state of anticipating either the next metaphorical thunderstorm, hurricane, or, worse yet, tsunami of stress related to their struggling adult child, it can really compromise their emotional health.

When Your Nervous System Becomes the Doppler Radar

Parents of struggling adult children often tell me they are exhausted. How would they not be? Sometimes, though, it isn’t primarily because of what their adult child is doing. It’s because of what these parents tell me they are anticipating. They get pulled into maddening overthinking loops such as these: Will she lose the job? Will he ask for money? Is she angry with me? Did I say too much? Should I text? Should I wait? What if he spirals? What if I don’t answer?

Staying with the weather metaphor, without realizing it, the parent’s nervous system becomes a kind of Doppler radar, constantly scanning the horizon for the next emotional storm. One of the most annoying things about this scenario is that the parent's radar occasionally works. It is agonizing for parents when they are "right" sometimes, because that's what makes the pattern so hard to break.

When the Forecast Starts Running the House

A mother I’ll call Susan noticed that she and her husband had stopped making weekend plans until they knew how their 34-year-old son was doing. If he seemed stable, they relaxed, but if he sounded discouraged, they stayed close to home. And if their son was angry (which was often the case), the entire weekend felt contaminated. During a coaching session with me, I gently asked Susan, “Why does his bad day have to become our bad day?” That question mattered because it helped Susan realize that compassion and emotional synchronization are not the same thing. You can care deeply that your adult child is struggling without requiring your own emotional state to match theirs.

article continues after advertisement

You Don’t Have to Control the Forecast

Parents sometimes believe peace will arrive when their adult child finally becomes more stable. Sure, I get why you would go there, but that gives another person (your adult child) enormous control over when your life gets to feel OK. I'm here to encourage you to consider a different goal.

Here's a caring, supportive newsflash for you: You can love your adult child without monitoring yourself and them 24/7. That means you can be aware of their storms without standing outside in them. And yes, you can answer the phone or respond to that text message without assuming you must fix what you hear.

No One Is Saying You Should Be Indifferent

In my work with parents of struggling adult children—and in my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! How to Stop Rescuing, Reduce Conflict, and Help Your Adult Child Move Forward—I often emphasize the difference between supporting an adult child and becoming responsible for keeping their life emotionally regulated. This means learning that you can have emotional separation with love. Let me put it another way: You can pay attention to your adult child's weather without making it your climate.

The Takeaway

Yes, your adult child may still have storms. So remember: The healthier goal isn’t to stop the rain. Rather, it’s to stop living every day with your eyes fixed on the radar.

item.title: 4 Ways to Practice Mindfulness on Your Wedding Day
item.description:
Mindfulness

4 Ways to Practice Mindfulness on Your Wedding Day

How to let mindfulness practice enhance your wedding day.

Posted August 18, 2026

We can define mindfulness as a present-focused, non-judgmental awareness. Functionally, mindfulness is all about being fully in the moment. You are not worrying about what will come next or ruminating about yesterday's problems; you're simply observing and taking in information. Mindfulness may be easy to describe but it can be more difficult to practice than it may seem.

What can mindfulness do for me on my wedding day?

Many things. Mindfulness helps you pay full attention to the present. That attention helps create strong and lasting memories. Your wedding day is absolutely one of those milestone moments you will want to be able to enjoy again and again. Being fully present will help you relive the day without relying on video or photos.

Mindfulness can also help reduce worry. If you have seen Inside Out 2, you know anxiety uses our imagination to project into the future (and typically focuses on possible catastrophes). Mindfulness strategies can help reduce that cognitive process. On your wedding day, fixating on all the possible problems will only steal your joy. If you are someone who runs a little anxious, mindfulness practices may help you take a little more enjoyment from the good things that do happen in the present.

Mindfulness strategies for your wedding day

  1. Ground through your senses. Nothing is more locked into the present than your five senses. Take a moment and run through all of them. Identify one thing you see, hear, feel, smell, and taste. This will connect you with the full picture of what is happening around you. It’s quick and will help you appreciate the end result of months of planning. I recommend a few wedding-specific mindful moments: If you have a bouquet of fresh flowers, close your eyes and smell them. During your first slow dance with your spouse, make sure you are mindful of your sense of touch and fully experience the embrace. (Pro tip: When using sensory grounding, sink into one sense at a time.)
  2. Put your phone away. Your phone is an anti-mindful device because it’s a distraction. Intentional virtual connection with someone who is unable to be physically present can be an exception, but it is still way too easy to get pulled into games or social media when your phone is in your hand. The virtual world will pull out of the present physical world. If your goal is to be mindful, build strong memories, and enjoy the day, your best bet is going to be keeping the phone away.
  3. Have 1-on-1 conversations. Take a little bit of time to connect personally, and really pay attention to the conversations so you can experience the happiness in the individual connections. An active conversation and appreciation of someone's presence will have a similar effect as sensory grounding. Depending on the size of the wedding, it is likely going to be impossible to dedicate 1-on-1 time to each person in attendance. Pick a few people you want to share a moment with, and then seek them out.
  4. Delegate to others. Delegating reduces the number of things that need to be in your working memory. It will give you more bandwidth and attentional control to remain in the present. You cannot simultaneously multitask and practice mindfulness. This can be a reason to hire a day coordinator, so logistics or problems can be delegated to them. Another good choice is to delegate things to the wedding party (or the spouse of someone in the wedding party).

From a planning perspective there is often a great deal of emphasis on photos and video from the day. These are of course wonderful mementos but there is also something powerful about your own memories. The strongest memories are the ones made mindfully. If you want to have a mindful experience, you will have to be flexible and bring some intentionality to your planning (e.g., delegating!). Being present also can mean letting go and relying a little more on trust. Trust that you have planned what you could, accept that some things will be out of your control, and participate in every moment fully.
